title: Trump invoked a zombie statute to justify tariffs on Canada
gist: PIIE's Alan Wm. Wolff argues the 2026 US tariffs on Canada rest on Section 338 of the 1930 Smoot-Hawley Act — a statute designed against colonial imperial preferences and dormant since the ITC last used it in 1943 — and should be struck down as the fourth failed legal theory after the emergency-powers, balance-of-payments, and forced-labor authorities. His operative point for investors: even repeated court losses won't stop tariff proliferation, because the administration will simply rotate to Section 301 and Section 232 cases already being planned, while Americans as importers of record bear the cost.

insights.claim: The 2026 US tariffs on Canada are justified under Section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, an antidiscrimination authority that PIIE's Alan Wm. Wolff calls a zombie provision the courts should reject as patently illegal.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: A tariff line built on the weakest legal footing yet is the most likely to be voided — asymmetric setup for Canada-exposed importers and cross-border supply chains if litigation lands.
insights.quote: They invoke a zombie authority found in the notorious and discredited Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, which deepened the Great Depression. The courts should reject these tariffs as patently illegal.
insights.locator: The world is used to American tariff news daily

insights.claim: Section 338 of Smoot-Hawley was written to counter blanket colonial-era trade discrimination — British imperial preference plus French, Dutch, Portuguese and Japanese colonial systems — not selective treatment of a few products, so its original purpose has no modern analogue.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Statutory-purpose arguments are the core litigation risk to this tariff; watch briefs that anchor on 1930s context rather than plain text.
insights.locator: Not to sound like the economics teacher in Ferris Bueller's class

insights.claim: Section 338 and its predecessor in the Fordney-McCumber Tariff Act of 1922 were designed as a deterrent against across-the-board retaliation by other countries, not as a tool for targeted product-level tariff actions.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: The deterrent-versus-rifle-shot distinction is the cleanest test a court can apply, and it cuts against a bilateral Canada action.
insights.quote: Section 338 was like a nuclear deterrent designed to provide leverage and forestall massive actions by others. It was not a statute for taking rifle shots but against across-the-board trade discrimination.

insights.claim: The International Trade Commission — the agency Congress designated under Smoot-Hawley to study and monitor alleged foreign discrimination — was not consulted before the 2026 Canada action, and its last activity under the statute dates to its 1943 Annual Report per Global Trade Alert.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: An 83-year procedural gap plus a skipped statutory fact-finder is the kind of record that gets tariffs vacated; a concrete date to cite in risk memos.
insights.quote: The last time the ITC did anything under this statute is cited in its 1943 Annual Report (according to Global Trade Alert).
insights.locator: Global commerce conditions today are much different

insights.claim: Some legal scholars argue Section 338 was effectively repealed by the enactment of Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, an implicit-repeal theory attributed to Philip Zelikow with additional misuse arguments from Harrell and Hillman.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Implicit repeal is an independent kill-shot that doesn't require the court to reach statutory-purpose arguments — raises the probability the tariff fails.
insights.locator: There are other legal theories the court can consult

insights.claim: The US Supreme Court held that the emergency-declaration authority used for an earlier round of Trump tariffs was not a tariff authority at all, killing the first of four successive legal theories.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: The top court has already foreclosed the broadest tariff instrument, forcing the administration into narrower and more litigable statutes.
insights.locator: First, it was the ill-fated tariffs under a declaration of emergency

insights.claim: The Court of International Trade found that the claimed balance-of-payments crisis used to justify a second round of tariffs did not exist.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Courts are willing to review the factual predicate, not just the legal authority — a meaningful constraint on future tariff design.
insights.locator: Then it was to deal with a claimed balance of payments crisis

insights.claim: A third tariff theory — retaliation against 60 countries of any size for tolerating forced-labor imports into their own markets — is still pending and about to be tested in court.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: A near-term binary litigation event with 60-country tariff scope attached; a decision date worth calendaring for global trade exposure.
insights.locator: The third try was retaliation against every country of any size

insights.claim: The Canada tariff represents the fourth distinct legal authority invoked in a rapid sequence and sets, in Wolff's assessment, a new record for lack of credibility among them.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Authority-shopping at this pace signals the constraint is legal creativity, not policy intent — model tariffs as persistent even when individual cases lose.
insights.quote: But the new tariffs on Canada set a new record for lack of credibility.
insights.locator: A new target is chosen, a new reason is put forward

insights.claim: Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 was the legally appropriate vehicle for acting against alleged Canadian harms to US commerce, but the administration made no Section 301 findings.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Choosing the wrong statute when a valid one exists is itself evidence of pretext — strengthens the case for judicial reversal.
insights.locator: Maybe there is some discriminatory Canadian treatment

insights.claim: The administration likely avoided Section 301 because the Administrative Procedures Act requires USTR decisions not to be arbitrary and capricious, a standard that is hard to meet given existing US violations of its own trade obligations.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Statutes with real evidentiary standards act as a brake; expect the administration to keep gravitating to authorities with no findings requirement.
insights.quote: Under the Administrative Procedures Act, which is applicable to the office of the United States Trade Representative, any decision taken by that agency must not be arbitrary and capricious to be valid.
insights.locator: But those findings were not made

insights.claim: US-Canada trade has been governed by mutually accepted agreements since NAFTA in the early 1990s and its Trump-administration successor USMCA, which removes the treaty vacuum Section 338 presupposed.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: USMCA is the operative legal frame; tariff actions outside it invite both domestic litigation and treaty-based Canadian responses.
insights.locator: Global commerce conditions today are much different

insights.claim: Any selective Canadian measures against US goods are plausibly defensive responses to the United States violating its own commitments, not the blanket discrimination Section 338 was written to punish.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Framing Canadian measures as reactive undercuts the discrimination predicate and reframes escalation risk as US-initiated.
insights.locator: It is therefore necessary to read the provision in the context of its time

insights.claim: The US tariff rate is currently whatever the president wishes it to be, with courts reduced to treating each claimed authority as valid until individually struck down — a structural lag that makes litigation an ineffective constraint.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Don't price tariff relief off court wins; the policy resets faster than judgments arrive, so assume a persistent tariff floor.
insights.quote: the fact is that at present the US tariff is whatever the president wishes it to be, which leaves the courts playing whack-a-mole, treating use of each claimed authority as sound—until it is found to be otherwise
insights.locator: Whatever the legal pretext that is chosen by the president

insights.claim: New tariffs will continue to be applied and will proliferate through individual Section 301 and Section 232 cases that are already being planned, even if the broader authorities keep losing in court.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Watch the Section 232 and 301 case docket as the forward pipeline of sector-specific tariff risk, rather than headline emergency actions.
insights.quote: New tariffs will continue to be applied and will proliferate, even if through use of individual Section 301 or Section 232 cases. They are already being planned.
insights.locator: Whatever the legal pretext that is chosen by the president

insights.claim: The Section 338 revival was driven less by legal strategy than by opportunism — in Wolff's reading, it was simply something the administration could not resist trying.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: If statute selection is opportunistic rather than strategic, obscure and dormant authorities become live tail risks for any trading partner.
insights.quote: Apparently, it was simply something the administration could not resist trying.
insights.locator: Other trade experts detail additional arguments

insights.claim: Tariffs on Canada are paid to US Customs by American importers of record, not by Canadians, despite the political framing of the measure as an action against Canada.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Model the tariff as a US cost shock on importer margins and consumer prices, not as a transfer extracted from Canada.
insights.quote: But it is Americans that have to pay the tariff to US Customs. They are the importers of record.
insights.locator: One last point. We all too readily see the newest tariff

insights.claim: Higher costs or outright unavailability of Canadian inputs can shut down American production lines and make other American products less competitive, making the tariff a supply-side disruption rather than only a price effect.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Screen US manufacturers with single-sourced Canadian inputs for production-halt risk, not just for margin compression.
insights.quote: With increased costs or even lack of availability of Canadian inputs, American production lines may shut down, while other American products may become less competitive.
insights.locator: One last point. We all too readily see the newest tariff

insights.claim: The precedent being reanimated — Smoot-Hawley — is the same 1930 law credited with deepening the Great Depression, an association Wolff invokes to argue the adverse economic consequences fall on the United States and its allies alike.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Historical framing matters for policy reversal odds: the more the Smoot-Hawley analogy sticks politically, the higher the pressure to unwind.
insights.quote: There are serious adverse economic consequences as well, for ourselves, for our friends.
insights.locator: With the latest tariff threat, Americans got more than an old movie
